title: Label alchemy: Target engineering for improved stock selection
abstract: Machine-learning research on stock returns has focused its attention on features and models, while treating the prediction target (or label) as a given (forward monthly or annual returns most of the time). We show that the choice of labels is crucial. Holding the investable universe (1,960 US stocks), the 122 firm features, and the model fixed, we decompose the label into location, scale and shape operators, combine them in a factorial design, and attribute out-of-sample stock-selection performance to each operator. Reshaping the target alone raises the long-short decile Sharpe ratio from 0.68 (simple return label) to 1.69 for the Gaussianised cross-sectional rank of that same return. These gains are model independent: replacing trees with a linear model or neural networks leads to the same conclusion. The label explains much more of the out-of-sample variation than the model does. We thus conclude that the prediction target deserves the same engineering effort that the field already devotes to models and features.
why: Label beats model for stock selection, 1.69 Sharpe out-of-sample

title: Prices or implied volatilities? Choosing the loss function in machine learning option pricing
abstract: This paper investigates the importance of the loss function in machine learning option pricing by asking whether a model should be trained on pricing errors or on implied-volatility errors. Both choices appear in the literature, usually without justification, and a meta-analysis of the field shows an increasing share of studies training on implied-volatility errors, whilst pricing accuracy remains the criterion on which their models are judged. We answer the question empirically by estimating the same machine learning model under two loss functions that differ only in the space where the error is measured, using 8.67 million S&P 500 index-option observations priced out of sample from 1997 through 2025. The price-space loss lowers pooled pricing RMSE by 25.3%, nearly twice what the network itself contributes over the parametric benchmark, and attains a lower error in every sample year and on the implied-volatility criterion that its rival optimizes. Conditional predictive ability tests show that the advantage varies with contract vega but not with market volatility, so it follows from the loss function rather than the sample period. The training space is therefore a first-order design choice, and researchers who price options with machine learning are better off measuring the error where the model will be judged.
why: Price vs IV loss function, 25.3% RMSE win, 8.67M options

title: Agentic AI as a Lens on Human Decision Making: Field Experimental Evidence from Dynamic Pricing
abstract: Agentic AI increasingly makes autonomous managerial decisions, yet little is known about what full delegation to AI reveals about human decision-making in high-stakes operations. Using large-scale field experimental evidence from a major Chinese airline, in which pricing authority on selected routes was delegated to an AI pricing agent, we compare autonomous AI pricing with decisions made by experienced human price setters. AI delegation increases revenue per available seat kilometer by 5.8% and adopts a qualitatively different intertemporal pricing strategy: instead of following the canonical ramp-up fare ladder, it sets relatively higher fares early in the booking horizon and lower fares close to departure. Auxiliary evidence suggests that the assumptions about consumer price sensitivity underlying the conventional ramp-up path are not always aligned with realized intertemporal booking responses. Using AI as an alternative operational benchmark, the AI-human performance gap provides a lens on two distinct sources of constraints on decision making: human decision routines under uncertainty and the AI's bounded information environment. The AI advantage widens under demand, strategic, and operational uncertainty, consistent with greater reliance on established decision routines under uncertainty, but narrows when economically relevant contextual information is difficult for AI to observe, highlighting the value of human contextual knowledge. These findings establish a diagnostic role for agentic AI: departures from incumbent practices can reveal underlying assumptions, decision routines, and information boundaries that are otherwise difficult to observe. An important implication from our research is that the AI performance gain may be transient, particularly when the value derives from exploiting expectations shaped by incumbent practices, but its diagnostic value persists as AI adoption reshapes the behavioral regularities and decision environments from which those gains arise.
why: Real agent airline pricing, 5.8% revenue gain, beats human strategy

title: Inflation narratives and risk premia
abstract: Theory suggests inflation risk premia are positive when supply shocks are expected to dominate demand shocks and negative otherwise. We measure these beliefs using demand and supply narratives derived from inflation news via Causality Extraction, which identifies causal relations between inflation and its drivers. Using narrative extracted from inflation news from the Financial Times for the Euro Area and the Wall Street Journal for the US, our key variable, NetDemand, measures the difference in articles attributing inflation to demand versus supply factors. Consistent with asset pricing theory, inflation risk premia are inversely related to NetDemand across maturities in both regions. This relationship holds even after controlling for the composite PMI and VIX, strengthens with risk aversion in the US and inflation volatility in the Euro Area, and is not subsumed by other measures of demand and supply contributions to inflation, views of professional forecasters, or narratives obtained from LLMs.
why: Text narratives predict inflation risk premia, real news data

title: LLM-Based Semantic Surprises in FOMC Communication: Asset Prices and Financial-Market Stress
abstract: This paper develops real-time semantic surprises from Federal Open Market Committee statements and studies how textual innovations enter asset prices and macro-financial stress. A fine-tuned transformer maps each sentence into stance probabilities and contextual embeddings; expanding-window forecasts separate unexpected hawkishness from unexpected semantic novelty. We match 225 statements from 1999 to 2026 to public 30-minute event-study data and the Office of Financial Research Financial Stress Index. Across equities, foreign exchange, nominal Treasury yields, real yields, and inflation compensation, conventional target and policy-path surprises dominate immediate price discovery. Semantic novelty is not a generic same-minute return factor. Its information appears in subsequent financial-stress dynamics and is strongly state dependent. In high-stress states, a one-standard-deviation novelty surprise is followed by declines of 0.30 index points on the release day, 0.86 after five trading days, and 0.94 after ten days; calm-state responses are small and short lived. Credit, funding, and volatility components all contribute to the adjustment, and the result strengthens continuously with pre-event stress and during NBER recessions. Recursive forecasts that allow novelty to interact with the stress state reduce five- and ten-day mean squared forecast errors by 22% and 23% relative to a benchmark containing conventional policy surprises and lagged financial conditions. The evidence identifies semantic novelty as a state-contingent macro-financial signal whose value emerges after initial price discovery.
why: FOMC semantic surprises beat conventional surprises

title: Welcome to the Factor Zoo: Where Mutual Fund Alpha Hides
abstract: This paper revisits the "no-alpha" view of active mutual funds. I estimate alphas using both the Fama-French model and LASSO-selected benchmarks drawn from 213 tradable factors. LASSO allows the selected factors to vary across funds and over time, producing a strategy-relative performance measure based on each fund's revealed exposures. The resulting benchmarks are parsimonious (with a median of seven factors) and economically interpretable. LASSO delivers better in-sample and out-of-sample performance and near-zero alpha for passive funds. The conclusions differ sharply: mean net active alpha is +9 b.p. per month under LASSO (and is persistent), versus-13 b.p. under the Fama-French model. The cross-sectional median of the LASSO-based active alpha exhibits a downward trend, consistent with the rise of passive investing. Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the manuscript preparation process. During the preparation of this work, the author used OpenAI's ChatGPT in order to proofread the manuscript and assist with optimization of the empirical analysis code. After using this tool, the author reviewed and edited the content as needed and takes full responsibility for the content of the manuscript.
why: LASSO factors beat FF3; practical implications

title: The RAMM Framework: Supervised Sequence Modeling for High-Frequency Market Making
abstract: Automated market making and High-Frequency Trading (HFT) require highly resilient models capable of processing high-dimensional limit order book (LOB) data and adapting to rapidly changing market microstructure regimes. While those traditional stochastic control models, such as the one by Avellaneda and Stoikov, offer solid mathematical grounds, they often make static assumptions about volatility and order arrivals, that are frequently broken in today's highly fragmented cryptocurrency markets. In this paper, we introduce a novel Supervised Sequence Modeling framework for continuous market making that uses Deep Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks as its foundations and compare its outcomes with the performance of a high efficient baseline of LightGBM Decision Trees. An important challenge to the use of Deep RL in financial time series is its strong tendency for overfitting: neural networks can quickly learn asset-specific correlations instead of the general microstructure dynamics. We scrutinize whether cross-asset zero-shot transfer learning (e.g., training with only Bitcoin (BTC) order flow and deploying a pre-trained model without changes on Ethereum (ETH) or Solana (SOL) would serve as a very strong form of regularization. Based on an in-depth simulation using billions of ticker-level events of Binance USD-M Futures data spanning from May 15th till 31st December 2023 for model creation while 1st January till 31st March 2024 for testing, empirical experiments demonstrate higher risk-adjusted performance of transfer models in comparison with inherently trained models in many tested cases. Especially in the LightGBM tree architecture, which has been empirically found to have a chronic "aggressive gamma" problem. In fact, the low value (γ = 0.01) is the most aggressive quoting scheme, which the decision tree models chronically underestimated to be the case. Instead, the LSTM architecture showed vastly better risk management and lower adverse selection practices, by dynamically adjusting its risk aversion to market conditions based on a temporal memory of volatility bursts, under a 2-bps synthetic fee stress test.
why: Relevant HFT domain, but results not shown

title: Structural Vulnerability in the AI Investment and Revenue Network: From Pilot Study to a Disclosure-based Extension
abstract: As of 2026, commonly cited CAPE measures for the S&P 500 are roughly 40-42, a range previously approached only around the dot-com peak. This study applies a DebtRank-style contagion model-originally developed for banking networks-to disclosed revenue links among AI value-chain firms, propagating a hypothetical spending-cut shock. An initial Pilot Study (18 nodes) suggested that counterparty revenue concentration is an interpretable indicator of financial fragility, but most of its edge weights relied on press-based estimates. This revised study makes four changes. (1) Every revenue edge carries an evidence label (Tier A/B) based on SEC filings and credible analyst or media attribution; edges without such support are dropped. (2) The network is expanded to 55 nodes by snowball sampling, of which 26 lie on at least one disclosed revenue edge. (3) Contingent backstop commitments, whose totals had been entered as annual payments in an earlier version of the model, are separated from ordinary revenue flows; one revenue edge (a $10B chip order) is re-attributed from OpenAI to Anthropic; and the status of the Nvidia-OpenAI $100B letter of intent is updated. (4) The network score follows the original DebtRank definition, which excludes the initial shock. Under the disclosed links, OpenAI has the largest spillover among the seven shock origins examined (2.4× the runner-up) and ranks first in all 2,000 perturbation draws. In the OpenAI scenario, AMD's damage exceeds Oracle's in about 91.5% of draws, but this ordering is sensitive to revenue-basis and annualization assumptions that the perturbations do not cover. The revenue links form an acyclic graph and equity links are not propagated, so the model does not test circular feedback among investment and purchasing flows; the results are best read as a disclosure-based mapping of concentration risk, not as a forecast or a test of the "circular financing" narrative. Code and generated results are reproduced in Appendix A.
why: Network analysis of AI fragility; SEC-disclosed edges

title: Algorithmic Collusion by Reinforcement-Learning Pricing Agents: Simulation Evidence and Implications for Financial Markets and Competition Law
abstract: Pricing algorithms built on reinforcement learning can reach supracompetitive outcomes with no agreement and no communication between the firms that deploy them. I report an independent simulation of Q-learning agents in a Bertrand oligopoly with logit demand and connect the results to competition policy for financial markets. Across 32 duopoly sessions the mean collusion index is 0.778, with a 95 per cent confidence interval of [0.735, 0.821] and per-firm profits 40 per cent above the Bertrand-Nash benchmark. Not one session ended at the competitive outcome. In a separate experiment on a common price grid, the index falls from 0.807 with two agents to 0.577 with three and 0.471 with four, while the relative profit gain over the competitive benchmark rises from 40 to 69 per cent. A forced deviation to the competitive price triggers a price war in the next period and a return to the previous level within five to seven periods. Removing the rival's past price from the state space eliminates the effect: the index drops to-0.018, with a confidence interval that contains zero, and prices settle at the static equilibrium. Coordination here follows from what the algorithm observes. Neither Section 1 of the Sherman Act nor Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union reaches conduct of this kind, and the RealPage proposed final judgment of November 2025 governs data inputs and tool design, leaving autonomous learning untouched.
why: RL collusion simulation, collusion 0.778, but not real market

title: When Managerial Tone and Performance Diverge: Implications for Downside Market Beta
abstract: Our study examines whether managerial tone–performance deviation affects firms’ downside market beta. Prior research examines tone levels, tone changes, and residual-based abnormal tone. We instead examine the distance between managerial tone and contemporaneous operating performance. Using MD&A text from Chinese A-share listed firms, we measure tone–performance deviation as the absolute difference between the decile rankings of MD&A net tone and operating profit margin within each industry-year. We find that greater managerial tone–performance deviation leads to a higher downside market beta over the 12 months following annual report announcements. The result is robust to alternative measures of operating performance, an LLM-based measure of managerial tone, additional controls and timing tests, alternative definitions of downside market states, alternative sample-screening rules, and the exclusion of major market-shock periods. Mechanism analysis shows that greater managerial tone–performance deviation increases investor disagreement. The effect of tone–performance deviation is stronger when managerial language certainty is higher, but weaker when the stock is eligible for short selling and when institutional ownership is higher. Our study extends the managerial tone literature by examining managerial tone jointly with contemporaneous operating performance.
why: Tone-performance misalignment predicts downside beta; real data, incremental.

title: The Effect of AI Adoption on Earnings Quality: Evidence from S&P 500 Technology Firms
abstract: This study examines whether the extent to which firms discuss Artificial Intelligence (AI) in their annual reports is associated with the quality of their reported earnings. Traditional financial reporting depends heavily on managerial judgment, while previous research has shown that the language used in corporate filings can contain information beyond the financial statements themselves (Loughran & McDonald, 2011). However, relatively little empirical research has directly examined whether AI-related disclosure is connected to earnings quality, particularly during the period following the rapid rise of generative AI. To investigate this relationship, I constructed a balanced panel of S&P 500 technology firms covering the study period. AI disclosure intensity was measured through keyword-frequency analysis of Form 10-K filings, while earnings quality was proxied by the absolute value of discretionary accruals estimated using the Modified Jones Model (Dechow et al., 1995). The analysis controls for firm size, leverage, profitability, growth, and year effects. The results indicate a statistically significant negative association between AI disclosure intensity and absolute discretionary accruals. Because lower absolute discretionary accruals are interpreted as higher earnings quality, the findings suggest that firms with more extensive AI-related disclosure tend to report higher-quality earnings. These results contribute to the growing literature on textual analysis of corporate disclosures and provide potentially useful information for investors, auditors, and regulators evaluating AI-related corporate communication.
why: Solid text analysis work but not actionable

title: Does AI Adoption Moderate Monetary Policy Transmission to Employment?
abstract: This dissertation asks whether AI adoption intensity moderates firm-level employment responses to identified monetary policy shocks, and whether that moderation emerged as AI diffused across US firms after 2020. It extends the firm-heterogeneity framework of Ottonello and Winberry (2020) to a technological dimension, combining a Compustat firm panel, Bauer and Swanson (2023) monetary policy shocks, and an AI-adoption proxy built from SEC 10-K disclosure text. Over the full 2017-2023 sample, AI adoption intensity does not significantly moderate employment responses to monetary shocks. Post-2020, a positive relationship emerges across every specification and robustness check attempted: AI-intensive firms show smaller employment contractions following contractionary shocks. This pattern survives an alternative shock series, a sectoral placebo test, and a healthcare boundary case. Standard firm-clustered inference reports the pattern as significant. An exact wild cluster bootstrap that accounts for the small number of independent year-level shocks post-2020 does not confirm significance at conventional levels, a limitation reported directly rather than smoothed over. The dissertation documents a consistent, theoretically coherent post-2020 pattern whose statistical confirmation is limited by how few independent policy episodes are available, with implications for how policymakers read labourmarket slack as a signal of policy transmission.
why: Real macro data, Compustat panel; but labor econ, not finance ML.

title: Temporally Governed Machine Learning for Bank Capital Monitoring and Supervisory Triage
abstract: Public bank data can support condition monitoring, advance prediction and scarce-capacity review, but success in one task does not establish success in the others. We report two independently governed retrospective studies of US regulatory bank data from 2004 to 2024. P3 forecasts four-quarter equity-to-assets and converts realised forecast errors and stress measures into a sequential monitor. In 55,869 bank-quarter observations from 2021–2023, its frozen q95 rule attains 84.56% precision, 77.10% recall and 95.95% specificity; because the four-quarter outcome is already observed, this is ex-post monitoring, not advance failure prediction. A separate origin-time P3 classifier is weak in the 2023 holdout (PR-AUC 0.0555; ROC-AUC 0.4915) and is descriptively outperformed by low current capital. GRAIL independently ranks four-quarter capital deterioration and conditional recovery under a deterministic within-quarter Top-5% review rule. In the 2021–2023 locked evaluation, deterioration selects 2,783 of 56,095 evaluable rows and captures 1,271 of 11,737 events (precision 45.67%; capture 10.83%), versus 582.3 expected captures under exact full-universe random review, a 2.18-fold lift. Recovery shows no corresponding enrichment (187 observed versus 188.1 expected). Deterioration capture varies from 5.53% in 2021 to 44.33% in 2023, and temporal reliability diagnostics reject a stable probability interpretation. The evidence supports governed risk ranking and retrospective surveillance research, not a combined deployed system, legal-failure prediction, causal effects or demonstrated supervisory benefit.
why: Bank capital prediction fails (0.055 PR-AUC), negative result

title: Forecasting Realized Volatility Using Idiosyncratic and Systematic Jump Risks: A Machine Learning Approach with Market Regimes
abstract: Accurate forecasting of equity market volatility is essential for risk management, portfolio allocation, and derivative pricing. From a machine learning and soft-computing perspective, this paper investigates the relative predictive role of idiosyncratic and systematic jump risks in forecasting realized volatility across major U.S. equity market sectors, considering both volatility levels and directional movements. We conduct a comprehensive out-of-sample comparison of linear benchmark models and a broad set of machine learning methods. The results show that selected machine-learning models improve forecasting accuracy relative to HAR, but the gains depend on the sector and algorithm, and HAR remains a competitive benchmark. Feature importance analysis indicates that systematic jump risk contributes more strongly to volatility predictability than idiosyncratic jump risk. To further capture nonlinear and timevarying market dynamics, we propose novel regime-dependent predictors derived from a Markov regimeswitching framework and incorporate them into the learning process. These regime-sensitive features lead to a marked improvement in forecasting performance, particularly for volatility direction prediction. Overall, the findings demonstrate that integrating jump-based feature engineering and regime-dependent information within machine learning frameworks yields more accurate and robust volatility forecasts.
why: Volatility forecasting; HAR remains competitive baseline

title: Pricing and Competition in Generative AI Ecosystems
abstract: The rapid adoption of generative AI (Gen AI) technologies has given rise to a distinctive dual pricing structure that differs from traditional digital services, driven by the high marginal costs of inference for every user interaction. A key feature of this emerging ecosystem is a vertical pricing mismatch where upstream Gen AI service providers typically charge usagebased (token-based) fees, while downstream AI application providers rely on subscription pricing for end users. This paper develops an analytical model of a two-tier digital value chain to study the economic implications of this pricing interaction. We characterize equilibrium prices, demand, and profits, considering consumer heterogeneity in usage and willingness to pay. The analysis reveals how upstream usage-based pricing shapes the subscription design, market coverage, and revenue outcomes of the application provider, and identifies conditions under which double marginalization and demand distortion arise. Our findings shed light on vertical contracting with asymmetric pricing schemes, heterogeneous usage, and platform-based services-settings that are increasingly central in AI-driven markets. From a practical perspective, the results offer guidance for Gen AI service providers and application developers on how to design pricing contracts, as well as insights for industry stakeholders and policymakers concerned with market power and innovation incentives of the Gen AI ecosystem.
why: Theoretical model, no empirical data

title: The Fragile Bourse, Identical Algorithms How Epistemic Homogeneity Triggers Order-Book Evaporation and the Illusion of Portfolio Diversification
abstract: Over the past three decades, global financial exchanges have transitioned to electronic order books governed by automated execution. As a result, sophisticated institutional allocators, such as Family Offices and Multi-Manager Hedge Funds, have adopted quantitative finance based on the premise that distinct mathematical models produce non-correlated return streams, consistent with Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT). Drawing on the Theory of Algorithmic Financial Cognition (TAFC), this paper demonstrates that this assumption is structurally flawed. Contemporary quantitative asset management faces a significant crisis of algorithmic homogeneity. Portfolios that appear diversified are, in fact, linked to similar model genealogies, primarily transformer-based and gradient-boosted architectures, rely on concentrated third-party data vendors, and are hosted on overlapping hyperscale cloud infrastructures. During non-linear market shocks, this structural convergence induces epistemic herding, resulting in abrupt and reflexive liquidity withdrawals that deplete order books. To address the disconnect between academic theory and practical capital preservation, this paper applies the Salih Index for Algorithmic Diversity (SIAD) as a portfolio defense mechanism for institutions and outlines a practical Algorithmic Epistemic Audit Protocol for Chief Investment Officers (CIOs).
why: Algorithmic homogeneity thesis lacks empirical evidence

title: How Much Is Unmeasured Housing Quality Worth? A Multimodal AI Framework for Measurement, Valuation, and Intervention in Bangkok
abstract: Many housing qualities that shape market judgments are not routinely encoded in structured property records, limiting their incorporation into hedonic analysis. This study develops a threestage multimodal large language model (MLLM) framework to measure conventionally unmeasured housing-quality attributes, estimate their asking-price capitalization, and translate interpretable physical cues into potential improvement scenarios. Using 2,601 apartment and 1,453 house listings in Bangkok, we derive exterior quality (EQ), interior quality (IQ), and neighborhood quality (NQ) from listing photographs and Google Street View images. An image benchmark assessed independently by five trained raters was used to compare 12 model-prompt configurations. The selected ChatGPT-4o configuration achieved a pooled held-out MAE of 0.707. Adding the three quality attributes increases within-grid adjusted R² by 0.054 for apartments and 0.031 for houses. A one-standard-deviation increase in EQ and IQ is associated with 17.2% and 21.8% higher apartment asking prices and 19.4% and 16.2% higher house asking prices, respectively. NQ is significantly capitalized for apartments (10.3%) but not for houses (1.8%). Apartment EQ is also more strongly capitalized in lower-priced than higher-priced local markets (15.0% versus 6.9%). Finally, 60 recurring object-state cues, classified by controlling actor, identify actionable conditions associated with higher quality, and generative AI-based controlled visual manipulations translate targeted improvements into changes in measured quality and modelimplied asking-price scenarios. The framework expands the measurable attribute space of hedonic analysis while linking measurement, valuation, and actionable intervention, thereby supporting...
why: Good MLLM method but wrong domain: real estate

title: Decision Half-Life Context Decay, Authority Drift and Replayable Controls in Tokenized and Agentic Finance
abstract: Financial systems are becoming continuous faster than investor context is becoming continuous. Tokenized securities can move across new market rails and representations, U.S. equity markets are preparing for longer operating windows, and artificial intelligence systems are progressing from recommendation toward multi-step action. Yet many investor-facing decisions still rely on a state of the investor, portfolio and authorization framework captured at an earlier point in time. This paper introduces Decision Half-Life as a research construct for measuring how long the context underlying a financial decision remains sufficiently valid before a material change requires revalidation. It develops three related concepts: Context Decay, where accurate information loses decision relevance as facts change; Authority Drift, where an automated system remains technically authorized while the factual context supporting the action has changed; and Decision Replayability, where a supervisor can reconstruct the state, evidence, material change, authority boundary, human intervention and outcome after an event. The framework is designed for the convergence of tokenized securities, near-continuous market infrastructure and agentic investment workflows. It separates asset and infrastructure revalidation from investor-context revalidation, proposes a technology-neutral control loop based on detection, selective revalidation, escalation and preserved evidence, and establishes an empirical programme for measuring detection latency, material-event recall, alert burden, authority drift and replay completeness. NeuFin's current research environment provides an initial instrumentation base for this work, including market events, portfolio positions, regime observations, audit records, market snapshots and decision records with fields for priority, suitability findings, evidence, data quality and human review. The paper's central argument is that time is becoming a first-class dimension of decision assurance: the question is no longer only whether a decision was authorized or well-supported when it began, but whether the context supporting it remains materially valid when action occurs.
why: Decision Half-Life framework, no empirical work

title: Does the AI Bill Pay Off? A Capital-Recovery Analysis of AI Data Centers
abstract: AI data centers combine long-lived power infrastructure with rapidly repriced computing equipment. This paper studies the capital-recovery conditions of this asset mix using a transparent annual project-finance model. The analysis separates energization dates, GPU procurement timing, billed utilization, hardware replacement, and financing cash flows. Two established discounted-cash-flow identities clarify why a relative improvement in project value need not make an investment acceptable, and why postponing a lossmaking investment can make its net present value less negative. In an illustrative one-gigawatt U.S. case, staged procurement produces an after-tax project NPV of -$12.93 billion at a 12% discount rate. Purchasing the same IT equipment before power is available reduces NPV to -$18.16 billion. The first-generation launch price required for zero NPV rises from $6.37 to $7.98 per GPU-hour. A 324-configuration deterministic grid evaluates the dependence of these findings on prices, utilization, power dates, connection spending, and replacement intervals. Only 33 configurations have positive NPV, a property of the selected grid rather than an estimated probability of success. A separate pre-tax comparison against a hypothetical flat 5% opportunity-cost benchmark avoids comparing after-tax project returns with pre-tax bond yields. The findings are conditional financial calculations, not estimates of industry profitability or causal effects of grid policy.
why: AI data center capital recovery analysis

title: Thirty Years of the Technology Industry, From Dot-Com to ChatGPT: Its Strong Stories and Their Relation to Capital Expenditure
abstract: Every few years the technology industry tells itself a story strong enough to move hundreds of billions of dollars of capital spending. This paper reads thirty years of the industry's own annual reports to see what those stories did, and how far today's story has got against the last one at the same age. Every company in the S&P 500 between 1996 and 2026 that belongs to the technology chain is placed in one of six groups by what it sold, from the designers of chips to the utilities that power the data centres, and for each group and year the paper adds up what its members reported: capital spending, revenue, operating cash flow, operating income and the market value printed on the cover of the annual report, every figure taken as first filed. Twenty-seven stories are dated to the day and pointed at the groups they were about, beginning with the Telecommunications Act of 1996 and ending with the software sell-off of February 2026, and a rule written down before any number was computed records the year each group's prices, spending and revenue moved. The network build-out that began in 1996 sets the comparison. By its third year the builders were putting 24 cents of every sales dollar back into the network, they were spending nine tenths of the cash their operations produced and crossed that line the year after, and the market had taken back nearly a third of the share of the industry's value it gave the builders and their suppliers when the story arrived. If the AI build-out that began in 2022 is on the same path, those three signs should show now, three years in. One of the three shows. The AI spenders put 22 cents of each sales dollar into equipment and buildings, against the builders' 24 at the same age, a year before that build-out peaked. The other two do not. The spenders are paying out of their own operating cash at six tenths of what it produces, where the builders were at nine tenths and over the line the next year. And the market has left the second pair's share of the industry's value where it was when the story arrived, 72 percent then and 72 now, where the first pair's fell from 71 to 50. The suppliers differ in kind rather than in degree. The group registered as this story's suppliers is larger than the equipment makers ever were, 27 percent of the industry's revenue against their peak of 15, and it keeps 29 cents of operating profit on the dollar where the equipment makers' best year was 13. Most of that group's revenue is devices rather than compute: a narrower group of the four companies that sell the compute, added after the registration and marked wherever it appears, is 8 percent of revenue at 48 cents on the dollar. The one group building with outside money is the power companies, as it has been every year since 2012, and its spending against its own cash peaked in 2022 and has fallen since. The record, with every company, story, hand-read figure and rule, is published as data for the studies that will test what it suggests.
why: Tech narrative analysis; not actionable trading

title: A Comparative Analysis of Private Unicorn Valuations and Public Market Benchmarks
abstract: For unicorn startups, it is often unclear whether their valuations are similar to those seen in public stock markets. Here, I compare private unicorn valuations with public-company valuation measures across different industries. Unicorn data was taken from the Global Unicorn Startups 2026 dataset, while public-company data, including market capitalization, revenue, and enterprise value, was collected from Yahoo Finance. The analysis compares median unicorn valuations with public-company EV/Revenue multiples and market capitalizations within similar sectors. The results show that private and public markets do not always value industries in the same way. Food/Delivery and Mobility/Transport have high private unicorn valuations despite relatively low public-market revenue multiples, while Fintech/Payments and AI/Software have some of the highest public-market multiples. Most unicorns are valued between $1 billion and $10 billion. Company age also appears to have a weak association with valuation. These findings suggest that private-market investors place greater emphasis on expected future growth and market opportunities.
why: Valuation multiples comparison; descriptive not predictive

title: Machine Learning versus Econometric Forecasting in the Forex Market: Evidence from EUR/USD, GBP/USD, and USD/CAD
abstract: This study compares the performance of machine learning models and traditional econometric models in forecasting exchange rates. Using daily data from 2010 to 2021, two machine learning models — Random Forest (RF) and Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) — are benchmarked against an Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) model across three currency pairs: EUR/USD, GBP/USD, and USD/CAD. Price-based indicators, including moving averages, the Relative Strength Index (RSI), and Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD), form the feature set. Model performance is evaluated using Root Mean Square Error, Mean Absolute Error, Mean Squared Error, classification accuracy, cross-validation, panel diagnostics, and significance testing. The machine learning models reduce forecasting error by up to 30% and improve portfolio-risk detection by up to 20% relative to ARIMA. EUR/USD and USD/CAD show the strongest gains; GBP/USD's gains are smaller, consistent with political events and commodity-price shocks not being fully captured by price-based technical indicators. The results indicate that machine learning's forecasting advantage is regime-dependent rather than universal, and that deploying AI-driven forecasting responsibly requires attention to explainability, regulatory oversight, and the algorithmic-bias and systemic-risk implications of correlated model adoption across institutions.
why: ML forex 30% RMSE gain; no transaction costs

title: After Attention: The Economics of Markets Where the Buyer Is an Agent
abstract: The consumer economy runs in part on attention rent: margin that sellers extract because human buyers search a little, remember imperfectly, and respond to persuasion. As personal purchasing agents ("twins") take over consumer choice, the standard expectation is that this rent collapses. We model a market with a mixed population of human and agent buyers in which sellers choose price, consumer-directed advertising, and agent-directed optimization spend, and we show that the collapse is neither smooth nor complete. Four results follow from the structure of agent demand. First, because a well-informed agent's demand is close to winner-take-most in quality-adjusted price, sellers face a discrete choice between a human-exploiting price and an agent-competitive one, which produces a tipping point: in our simulations gross margin falls 1.4 percentage points as the agent share rises from 0 to 0.2, then drops from 40% to 33% by a share of 0.3 and to 4% when all buyers are agents. Second, we prove that in a duopoly benchmark a mixed population admits no pure-strategy equilibrium in the interior of a discrete price grid — a counterpart of Varian (1980), subject to a grid-fineness condition we state — and in the simulated market every convergent run sits at one of the two boundaries, which is what that mechanism predicts. Third, if agents are persuadable, advertising does not disappear but migrates: total persuasion spending peaks at 1.69 times the pre-agent advertising budget and remains above it when all buyers are agents. That migration does not chiefly misallocate demand — good sellers still win about 85% of sales either way — but it preserves seller rent (margin 9.9% against 4.0%) and concentrates the market by a factor of 2.4 (HHI 7,424 against 3,102). Consumer net value per unit also falls, and across the persuadability range it crosses from positive to negative in the neighbourhood of gamma = 1; we report that crossing rather than a percentage change, because the level of that series is an artifact of the value scale (Appendix C). Fourth, we measure the parameter the third result turns on. In a preregistered experiment of 18,000 purchase decisions across three frontier LLMs acting as buyers, one sentence of unverifiable promotional text raises a mid-ranked product's selection rate by a factor of 8 to 14, while a length-matched neutral placebo shows no detectable effect (z = -0.04, +1.18, +1.25) — and the share going to the genuinely best-value product falls on every model. A second preregistered experiment of 19,200 further decisions finds that this susceptibility does not detectably change when the buying instruction states urgency. Persuadability is therefore not an assumption of this paper but a measured property of the models tested. We also read the agentic-commerce protocols standardized between 2025 and 2026 — AP2, ACP, Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard Agent Pay and UCP — and find that they cryptographically secure payment authorization while leaving product claims unstructured and unattested, lowering the friction that governs adoption without touching the parameter that governs who captures the gains. Simulation code, both preregistrations, and all 37,200 measured decisions are public at https://github.com/sage7AI-explore/after-attention.
why: Agent buyer model theoretical, no real market data

title: Cited but Not Clicked: Evidence from a Cryptocurrency Exchange on the Value-Capture Gap in Generative Engine Optimization
abstract: The shift from ranked search results to AI-synthesized answers has been widely documented as a traffic threat to online publishers, and Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) has emerged as the industry's proposed response: optimizing content to be cited within AI answers rather than ranked as a clickable link. This paper tests an assumption embedded in that response: that citation-level visibility carries recoverable economic value, using twelve months of Google Search Console data from a real, anonymized cryptocurrency exchange ("Meridian Exchange"). We find that site-wide click-through rate (CTR) collapsed from 40.17% to 5.54% between a confirmed organic baseline period and a recent trough, and that this collapse persisted even among queries that held their search ranking position, ruling out conventional ranking decline as the primary explanation. A close reading of the query "meridian login" shows CTR falling from 49.9% to 6.0% across three periods while position remained effectively constant near rank 1. Direct inspection of the live search results page confirms a Google AI Overview citing Meridian Exchange by name while fully resolving the user's query inline, without requiring a click. We argue this reflects an underexamined mechanism: AI Overviews can intercept clicks not only on purely informational queries, as the existing literature assumes, but on branded, navigational queries that carry a hidden procedural sub-intent. The result is a citation that satisfies GEO's definition of success while capturing none of the economic value that citation has traditionally implied.
why: Crypto exchange search traffic; not financial ML method.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Improving Project Budgeting and Pricing Accuracy
abstract: Artificial intelligence AI is being used more often in finance, especially for tasks that involve large amounts of information and repeated calculations. One area where it may be useful is project budgeting and pricing. Companies usually prepare project budgets using past information, spreadsheets, and the experience of financial professionals. Although these methods are still widely used, they can become less reliable when a project is complicated or when market conditions change. AI offers another way to approach these tasks by analyzing large datasets, identifying relationships between different variables, and using them to produce estimates. This research compares traditional financial estimation methods with AI-supported approaches. The comparison looks at project cost estimation, budget accuracy, pricing decisions, and expected profit margins. Previous research suggests that AI-based models can reduce forecasting errors and make some parts of the estimation process faster. However, the results depend on the quality of the available data and on how the technology is implemented. Employee knowledge, implementation costs, and human review also remain important factors. The findings therefore suggest that AI can be used as an additional tool in financial planning rather than as a replacement for financial professionals. When it is introduced into existing processes properly, it can reduce some of the repetitive work involved in financial analysis while leaving the final decisions to people with the necessary financial knowledge and experience.
why: Vague position paper on budgeting

title: Public AI Wealth Funds and the Economics of Shared Ownership
abstract: Public ownership of artificial intelligence assets can broaden participation in technological gains without correcting the market power, data appropriation, and deployment harms that determine those gains. This paper develops the Public AI Wealth Fund proposed by deVadoss in August 2025 as an integrated public economics design. The fund acquires diversified stakes across the AI stack through subsidy-linked warrants and specified levies, preserves contributed principal, and pays universal dividends from realized returns. Independent competition enforcement, individual data rights, deployer accountability, and resource-use rules remain binding on portfolio companies. A tractable model separates the distribution of profits from the efficiency of their generation. Public ownership improves distribution under explicit welfare weights, but cannot remove monopoly deadweight loss; a smaller stake in a more contestable market can produce greater welfare than a larger stake in an unreformed market. Additional results characterize investment distortions, the conditions for labor-income hedging, and a payout rule that prevents distributions from deepening capital impairment. Comparisons with Sanders, Altman, broader social wealth funds, and debtfinanced AI investment distinguish ownership, control, financing, and payout commitments. The design's comparative advantage is conditional: it combines reciprocal public claims with institutional constraints on rent extraction and unfunded distributions. Numerical illustrations expose both this advantage and the limited scale of early dividends. The analysis establishes design conditions rather than an empirical ranking of enacted policies.
why: Theory-heavy policy paper: no implementation

title: Generative Capital: Foundations of AI-Native Personal Finance
abstract: The digitization of money has largely solved the problem of moving small amounts of value quickly. It has not solved the problem of allocating capital well. For many prospective investors, entry into financial markets, and into crypto-assets in particular, is impeded by price volatility, counterparty risk, operational complexity and a lack of transparency about what is owned and who stands behind it. Tokenization may lower some access barriers by making claims divisible, programmable and transferable, but access is not allocation capability: a larger accessible universe raises, rather than lowers, the decision burden placed on the investor. This paper introduces Generative Capital, a financial architecture that integrates tokenization, decentralized finance, artificial intelligence, quantitative portfolio construction and agents: (i) eligible assets are digitally represented and divisible, (ii) only assets, and counterparties, that pass structured and continuing legal and financial diligence enter the investable universe, (iii) natural-language investor intent is translated by an AI interpretation layer into explicit, auditable financial constraints, (iv) a deterministic allocation engine constructs portfolios under those constraints, and (v) specialized agents execute, monitor, rebalance and document the result as investor and environment change. In this combination, decentralized finance provides programmable infrastructure for access and transactions, while AI connects that infrastructure to investor intent and adaptive allocation. "Generative" refers to the generation of a personalized allocation from intent and verified opportunities, not to the creation of money or returns.
why: Roadmap for generative capital, no evidence

title: A HYBRID ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FRAMEWORK FOR REAL-TIME FRAUD DETECTION AND ADAPTIVE CYBER THREAT INTELLIGENCE IN FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS
abstract: Digital financial services, cloud banking, mobile payment systems, and real-time financial ecosystems have revolutionized the banking industry by making financial transactions quick and easy, and much more interconnected and accessible across the world (Chang et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2024). This digital transformation has, at a time, also expanded the attack surface for cybercriminals, leading to more sophisticated financial fraud schemes like account takeover, synthetic identity fraud, payment fraud, insider threats and even AI-assisted attacks which are often hard to stop with traditional rule-based security systems (Nicholls et al., 2021; Dharmireddi et al., 2025). Current fraud detection methods often lack the ability to detect new attack patterns quickly and at the same time keep a low false-positive rate, are transparent in the model and are capable of a real-time decision making. It is proposed that a comprehensive hybrid Artificial Intelligence framework with the integration of every aforementioned AI methodology mentioned in this study can be used to boost financial fraud detection and response (Alarfaj & Shahzadi, 2025; Rahman, Nurujjaman, & Hossain, 2025; Waheed et al., 2026). This proposed framework integrates behavioral analytics, relational transaction modelling, ongoing policy optimization and interpretable AI methods to identify known and unknown fraudulent activities in financial environments comprised of distributed applications. The framework combines adaptive threat intelligence and reinforcement learning, enabling it to continuously adapt its detection methodologies in response to new attack behaviors and ensuring transparency for regulatory compliance and trust building among stakeholders. The anticipated results are that fraud detection will be more accurate, false positive rates will be minimized, models will be more explainable, models will be deployed across financial infrastructures in the cloud, and they will continuously learn to improve the overall organizational cyber resilience to enable secure digital financial operations in complex financial ecosystems (Rahmati, 2025; Kumar, 2025; Muthukumarasamy & Srinivasan, 2025).
why: Vague fraud detection, sounds like position paper

title: Market Share Analysis for Closed-Weight and Open-Weight AI Models
abstract: Market definition and market share analysis are central elements of most antitrust assessments. In markets for AI models, however, challenges arise. Because of the variety of ways in which models are deployed, it is difficult to obtain data that cover the whole market and are commensurable. This article investigates how far market share analysis carries here. It specifically looks into turnover, token volume, model downloads, and web traffic. The core thesis is that, where comprehensive market share quantification fails, traditionally distinct analytical steps, namely market delineation, share quantification, and market power assessment, collapse into one unitary analysis of competition. This shows that, owing to insufficient data for market share measurements, the approach shifts from form-based to effects-based, and that further empirical research, especially using survey techniques, is required.
why: AI market share measurement; antitrust not trading

title: Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall: Measuring Tail Risk in a Technology Equity Portfolio
abstract: This paper applies Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (CVaR) to a portfolio of four large-cap tech stocks: Apple (AAPL), Alphabet/Google (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), and NVIDIA (NVDA). I pulled the actual daily price data from Yahoo Finance using the yfinance Python library with auto_adjust=True, which automatically corrects for stock splits and dividends so that each return reflects what an investor actually experienced. The data covers January 2, 2022 through December 31, 2024, giving 751 trading days. I chose this three-year window deliberately because it covers three structurally different market environments: the 2022 tech selloff, the 2023 recovery driven by AI, and the 2024 extended rally. Having all three in the same dataset makes the risk estimates more realistic and more robust than if I had only looked at a single market regime. The method I used is historical simulation. You sort the actual historical returns and read off the loss at a given quantile, without assuming any particular distribution. This is the most intuitive approach, and it is also widely used in practice because it captures the heavy tails and skewness that are present in real financial return data, especially for tech stocks. I chose an equally weighted portfolio to isolate the effect of diversification and risk measurement without introducing bias from a specific optimization strategy. Each stock receives a 25% weight, representing $25,000 each within a $100,000 portfolio. For this portfolio, the 1-day VaR at 95% confidence comes out to $3,139.14. That means on about one out of every 20 trading days (roughly 5% of the time), you’d expect to lose more than that amount. I also computed the Expected Shortfall (CVaR), which tells you how bad losses actually are on average on those worst days. At 95%, that number is $4,101.54, about 31% above the VaR threshold. That gap is the most important finding in this paper: VaR tells you where the threshold is, while CVaR shows how severe losses actually are once that threshold is crossed. In a tech-heavy portfolio, that difference has significant implications for risk management. The paper also breaks down the VaR for each individual $25,000 position, where NVDA alone carries nearly twice the tail risk of AAPL or MSFT. I also look at the diversification benefit you get from holding all four stocks together rather than treating each position separately, which comes out to $356.81, roughly a 10% reduction in risk. Finally, I extend the 1-day estimates to a 10-day horizon using the square-root-of-time rule, giving a 95% VaR of $9,926.83, which is consistent with Basel II and Basel III reporting frameworks. The limitations of historical simulation are discussed openly in the final section.
why: Textbook VaR/CVaR, no novelty

title: The Zytra AI Risk Atlas: A Structured Taxonomy of 141 Risks for Agentic and Foundation-Model AI Deployment in Banking and Financial Services Methodology, Coverage Architecture, Deployment-Pattern Tagging, and Benchmark Validation Against Peer Frameworks
abstract: Existing AI risk frameworks-including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, OWASP LLM and Agentic AI Top 10, MITRE ATLAS, and the MIT AI Risk Repository-provide partial coverage of the risk surface encountered in enterprise AI deployment, but none offer a unified, operationally structured taxonomy that simultaneously classifies agentic and non-agentic risks, maps to deployment-specific patterns, and is calibrated for the regulatory and harm context of banking and financial services. This paper presents the Zytra AI Risk Atlas (ZARA), a structured taxonomy of 141 named AI risks organised across 16 unified domains, of which 77 address risks specific to autonomous agentic AI systems and 64 address risks common to foundation-model deployments without autonomous agency. We describe the taxonomy design methodology, the rationale for the agentic/non-agentic distinction as a primary classification axis, the deployment-pattern tagging scheme that maps risks to specific architectural patterns (RAG, agentic orchestration, multi-agent pipelines, document extraction, summarisation), and the BFSI harm amplification taxonomy that assigns regulatory, financial, and reputational consequence scores to each risk. We benchmark ZARA against seven peer frameworks across five dimensions-taxonomy depth, agentic coverage, BFSI specificity, operational controls linkage, and enterprise governance support-and report dimension-level scores. We identify 13 net-new risk classes that emerged from global AI safety research in 2025-2026 not covered by any existing public taxonomy and describe the controls framework (UACF) that links each risk to testable, owner-assigned controls. ZARA and the UACF are available for academic and enterprise use at zytratechnologies.com.
why: Risk taxonomy reference, not actionable research

title: Thin Rallies, Heavy Sell-offs: A Fragility Ratio for When Price and Volume Tell Conflicting Stories About Stock Returns
abstract: To better understand what sits under the hood of returns, a conceptualization of fragility is needed first. This white paper posits that fragility-and not risk itself-comes from two market regimes: higher prices on lower volumes (hollow rally), and lower prices on higher volumes (deep breakdown). Taken together, these regimes can be informative about how the returns are obtained. A Fragility Ratio is proposed here, and it prints how much return an asset delivered per unit of fragility, narrowed down to these two regimes of volatility. Next, a Fragility Cost of Return is introduced, and it prints how much fragility an investor had to endure to obtain 1% of return. These insights are built upon the ratios proposed by Sharpe and Sortino, and the novelty of this paper lies in asking a narrower research question: What does an asset's fragility stemming from price and volume diverging from each other reveal on its own and in relation to the returns investors actually earn? To make these theoretical concepts visible and easy to use, the Fragility Ratio indicator was created using the code made available via Claude AI, and it is publicly available on TradingView for financial analysts, investors-institutional or retail-and journalists to use in their reports and articles.
why: Fragility ratio proposal; validation unclear

title: Money Doctors at Work Planning Quality, Financial Anxiety, and the Value of Financial Advice
abstract: We study the non-pecuniary value of financial advice. We document two results. First, the comprehensiveness of financial planning, not mere access to an advisor, is associated with lower financial-specific anxiety. This association is concentrated almost entirely among less financially literate households, the pattern predicted by the money doctors model of Gennaioli, Shleifer, and Vishny (2015), in which advice is most valuable to those facing the greatest uncertainty. Second, using within-person variation in the two-wave panel, we show that initiating an advisory relationship improves self-assessed financial management and that maintaining one improves financial satisfaction. Clients of certified (CFP) advisors receive more comprehensive service across all six planning domains, identifying credentialing as a determinant of advice quality. We find no evidence that AI-based financial tools substitute for human advisors. Our findings suggest that the value of financial advice lies in comprehensive planning and the management of financial anxiety.
why: Financial advisory value; not trading strategy

title: Decision Debt in AI-Generated Work: Preserving Observability, Traceability, Modularity, and Changeability
abstract: Artificial intelligence can produce work that is functionally correct at delivery yet difficult to inspect, reconstruct, or modify later. This paper develops the concept of decision debt for AI-generated work: the future cost created when an acceptable output is retained without preserving the assumptions, evidence, dependencies, and interfaces needed to understand and safely change it. The concept extends but does not replace technical debt. Whereas technical debt traditionally concerns implementation and architectural compromises that increase future maintenance cost, decision debt focuses on lost decision structure across software, analytical work, and agentic workflows. The paper proposes four preservation properties—observability, traceability, modularity, and changeability—and a future-changeability test for evaluating whether AI-generated artifacts remain governable after delivery. It also offers a qualitative decision-debt checklist and a risk-adjusted preservation heuristic for deciding how much reconstruction evidence to retain. It also distinguishes external reconstruction evidence from private model reasoning: maintainability does not require access to an AI system's hidden chain of thought, but it does require sufficient records of sources, actions, tests, assumptions, and artifacts to reconstruct consequential decisions. The contribution is integrative rather than a claim that provenance, maintainability, or technical debt are individually new. The central claim is that correctness is a present-tense property, while changeability is a future-tense property; reliable AI-generated work requires both.
why: Decision debt concept; no empirical validation

title: Fragmented by Design: Why Current AI Regulation Fails to Address Systemic Risk
abstract: The governance of artificial intelligence has entered a phase of legislative acceleration. In the space of three years, the European Union enacted the world's first comprehensive AI regulation, the United States published a voluntary risk management framework, the G7 produced an international code of conduct, and more than seventy countries initiated national AI policy processes. Yet speed of production has not translated into depth of coverage. A systematic comparative analysis of eight major AI regulatory instruments - the EU AI Act (2024), NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (2023), ISO/IEC 42001:2023, OECD AI Principles (2019, revised 2023), G7 Hiroshima Process (2023), the UK's pro-innovation framework, China's Generative AI Interim Measures (2023), and India's emerging MeitY policy framework, reveals three structural failures that no existing instrument resolves. First, accountability diffusion: when AI systems cause harm, no framework provides an unambiguous, enforceable chain of liability from developer through deployer to user. Second, dynamic risk invisibility: risk classification is performed at the point of deployment, while AI systems evolve, fine-tune, and drift post-launch without any binding obligation to re-assess. Third, a cross-border enforcement vacuum: AI systems are global; governance instruments are jurisdictional. No binding multilateral enforcement mechanism exists, and soft coordination frameworks such as the OECD Principles and G7 commitments produce normative alignment without operative effect. This paper argues that these three gaps are not incidental oversights correctable through incremental amendment. They are architectural features of how AI governance has been designed, jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction, framework-by-framework, in the absence of a shared foundational theory of AI liability, risk continuity, or international enforcement. The paper draws on a comparative matrix applied to all eight instruments, identifies four secondary gaps that compound the foundational failures, and proposes a tiered set of policy recommendations spanning immediate (0–2 year), medium-term (2–5 year), and long-term (5+ year) horizons. The central long-term proposal is the establishment of a global AI governance body with narrow but binding enforcement authority, modelled on the institutional architecture of FATF for financial crime and the IAEA for nuclear safety, precedents that demonstrate that technically complex, cross-border risk can be governed multilaterally when political will exists.
why: Survey of AI regulation frameworks; rejected category

title: Rebuilding the Climate Code for the Digital Age Coordinating the Reformation of Carbon Accounting and Environmental Markets to Scale the Transition Economy
abstract: Corporate carbon accounting and the verified carbon market (“VCM”) were built by different climate action communities, for different purposes, on incompatible logics. The dominant carbon accounting framework, the Greenhouse Gas Protocol (“GHGP”), treats greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions as information, as a company’s subjective view of its direct and indirect impact, not as a transactable legal object capable of embodying or representing the environmental performance of a company project or product in commerce. Environmental attribute certificate (“EAC”) markets like the VCM do the opposite. The VCM treats verified GHG reductions and removals as transferable intangible property, assets that are generated through a constitutive process that distinguishes and decouples the right to own and convey a defined environmental achievement from the measurement, reporting and verification (“MRV”) information evidencing it. The net result is carbon accounting that produces MRV data with no concept of property or transactability, and the VCM that produces transactable intangible property that is disconnected from its MRV data. Neither domain, as architected, connects and integrates climate action with business decision-making, and the friction between the two stunts demand for low-carbon investment. A new coordination architecture is needed to enable markets to scale the transition, one that connects property to environmental achievements with their evidentiary records, using an authoritative system of record. That first generation of these systems (known here as the “Climate Code”) did not build an architecture designed to scale. In fact, no coordination architecture was built. Systems change may therefore require no new physics, no carbon pricing scheme, no environmental mandate and no governmental intervention to get started. Only organized market governance around a common system of record infrastructure is needed, a cooperative utility system. Carbon accounting and the VCM therefore may not need to change what they do so much as how they do it. As this paper explores, climate-forward industries can start building cooperative institutions and digital infrastructure that run on a property-based, rules-based information coordination architecture for all types of EACs, synchronizing new “e-ledger” accounting conventions as the source code ontology for a market architecture whose system of record is administered by an independent operator. The system of record can be operated under a cooperative self-governance model established by industry for industry. Companies could then choose to manage carbon as an asset class and to use artificial intelligence to help constitute product-level emissions, carbon intensity scores and verified mitigation outcomes as EACs embodying property interests that can be transacted, pledged and collateralized. None of the foregoing diminishes the science-based integrity of the standards and methodologies used to measure emissions and emissions abatement. The answer for adoption lies in a system of record for the information, for the data that will fuel the transition. Verified product-level emissions data and reduction MRV data are both evidentiary records: artifacts a machine can read and a market can govern, warehoused as digital property within a system that recognizes and enforces rights of control and access. Seen that way, digitalization and decarbonization can and should become complementary megatrends driving the transition economy. Artificial intelligence and tokenization are then neither a fraud machine nor an edge-case perimeter question, but the means by which rights in a company’s environmental performance are married to its verified evidence, deposited and custodied in a closed-loop utility, and transacted at speed as an EAC title instrument. The answer to climate action is to link MRV records with the property rights to the environmental achievement on a common system of record
why: Carbon accounting frameworks, not core finance

title: Appraising AI Infrastructure as a National Technology Investment: A Welfare-Accounting Framework for Technology Sovereignty Applied to Saudi Arabia and Singapore (2026-2030)
abstract: Governments are committing capital to AI infrastructure technology faster than methods exist to judge whether it will pay off for their nations. This paper proposes the Social Net Present Value (SNPV), a bottom-up welfare-accounting framework for assessing emerging technology investment decisions in artificial intelligence infrastructure. The SNPV evaluates the net welfare impact of AI data centers by integrating five economic flows (sovereignty insurance value, domestic retained income, fiscal effect, labor income, and social resource cost) into a single discounted measure, split into a sovereign tier and a commercial tier. We apply the method across scenario-based deployment pathways for Saudi Arabia and Singapore, two contrasting national innovation strategies, and estimate whether, why, and under which conditions domestic AI infrastructure investment adds net national welfare. The SNPV pairs with a stress-test diagnostic, the Compute Viability Band (CVB), identifying the price band within which the technology investment stays viable. Over 2026-2030, both countries obtain comparable aggregate gains (≈USD 30 billion) under the planned deployment scenario, but through opposite compositions: Singapore's gain is almost entirely commercial, Saudi Arabia's combines commercial returns with technology-sovereignty insurance value. The framework equips policymakers to appraise AI infrastructure technology strategy under uncertainty and align emerging technology policy with national innovation goals.
why: Infrastructure investment framework; policy not trading

title: Vietnam-MNE Transfer Pricing Blockchain Surveillance Model in VN
abstract: Vietnam has become an attractive destination for multinational enterprises (MNEs), but this also raises significant risks of transfer pricing practices that erode tax revenues and distort fair competition. This study explores the application of blockchain technology as a strategic tool to monitor and control transfer pricing activities in Vietnam. Building on OECD transfer pricing principles and decentralized blockchain architecture, the research proposes the Vietnam-MNE Transfer Pricing Blockchain Surveillance Model. The model integrates AI-driven risk analysis, smart contracts, standardized data frameworks, and multi-layer authentication to ensure transparency, immutability, and real-time traceability of related-party transactions. By simulating internal transaction activities and analyzing current legal frameworks, the findings demonstrate that blockchain can reduce tax fraud, shorten audit time, and enhance compliance monitoring. This approach not only strengthens Vietnam's tax management capacity but also contributes to building a modern, fair, and digitalized tax ecosystem aligned with global standards.
why: Transfer pricing blockchain proposal, no data

title: Liability and Pricing of Dual-Use AI
abstract: How much liability should AI providers bear when their services enable both attack and defence? Liability can improve welfare while increasing harm. Providers sell a common input to productive users, attackers and defenders. Within a defended contest, a higher common price reduces effort without changing attack success or attacker profits, saving resources and improving the target's security payoff. Compensation weakens defence and raises attacker profits. Optimal liability balances these effects against productive exclusion. Greater competition can lower optimal liability; every such decline must end at an outcome retaining defence. With cybersecurity access fixed, monopoly can warrant partial liability but never full liability when provision is worthwhile. When guardrails preserving productive uses are available, strong competition favours universal guarding socially but encourages unilateral removal at insufficient liability. At a fixed provider count, sufficiently many productive users ensure a pure equilibrium with universal guarding under high liability. A universal-guarding requirement makes liability redundant. Under monopoly, adoption follows a unique liability threshold, while zero liability remains uniquely optimal for a range of parameters with sufficiently many productive users.
why: Pure theory on dual-use AI liability

title: Contract Choice and Commitment Concessions: Evidence from Individual-Level Electricity Consumption and Payments
abstract: Electricity bills are rising faster than inflation, making a household's electricity contract an increasingly consequential decision. Deregulated retail markets generally offer a choice between fixed rate contracts (FixRCs) and variable rate contracts (VarRCs), yet their financial impact is obscured by non-linear pricing, price volatility and consumers' self-selection based on their latent characteristics. To improve transparency of rates, utilities post representative rates corresponding to a few consumption levels in Electricity Facts Labels (EFLs). Methodology/results: In collaboration with one of the largest U.S. utilities, we estimate the causal effect of contract choice on realized rates for more than 77,000 households recorded over a full year, linking each household's rate to its contract, tenure, monthly and hourly consumption, and zip-level demographics. We find that rates tend to increase with consumption variability. We address self-selection by instrumenting contract choice with lagged Google search intensity for the state's electricity-shopping platform in a Two-Stage Least Squares and a Double Machine Learning (DML) frameworks controlling for the full consumption profile. FixRCs reduce rates by approximately 4¢/kWh, roughly one fifth of the average rate; the largest savings accrue to high-income households whose consumption concentrates in winter months, the signature of electric heating. Managerial implications: The FixRC discount (commitment concession) is substantial on average. Utilities can adjust the commitment concession to achieve a specific mix of FixRC and VarRC consumers. Moreover, they can reveal this concession to attract FixRC consumers, especially to those using electric heating. We make two concrete process recommendations to utilities i) enhanced EFLs with quotes based on consumption level and variability, and ii) break-even service length informing consumers about the contract length beyond which FixRCs become cheaper than VarRCs. Enhanced EFLs and break-even service length increase transparency and in turn can help lower-income households raise their savings closer to those of higher-income households, making the market fairer.
why: Off-topic: electricity utility contracts

title: The Effect of Changes in Insurance Companies' Strategies And Performance Quality on Their Value Relevance: (A Doubtful Vision for Artificial Intelligence Method for Future Real Recommended Inference)
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to recommend an artificial intelligence method that could help measure the effect of changes in insurance companies' strategies, and how far their performance quality will be, on their value relevance. The idea of this paper is derived from the issue of difficulty to obtain real and sufficient data from official websites presenting financial reports of insurance companies, which could help in conducting empirical research for insurance companies. In this paper, I discuss a method I label as a command-based artificial intelligence method (CBAIM), which generates insurance companies' accounting information derived from the insurance markets. Nevertheless, the method does not have sufficient accuracy to rely on for proving the rationality of the insurance companies' value relevance movement because of changes in insurance accounting information and the strategies behind such changes. In this paper, I raise the question of: How far could significant accounting information for insurance companies, under both IFRS and GAAP, drive insurance companies' capital stocks? Future research can work on an empirical method to use real and sufficient data if available, and compare the results to results from the method I recommend in this paper as CBAIM. My findings need additional studies, as neither real insurance companies' financial reports nor CBAIM have robust evidence to prove the rationality of the value relevance changes due to the effect of insurance companies changing strategies.
why: Incomplete insurance AI method, admits low accuracy

title: Sweat Equity in the Machine: Anticipatory Relationship Investment, Consumer Labor, and Strategic Lock-in in Consumer-AI Relationships
abstract: Why do consumers remain committed to a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) agent that currently underperforms available alternatives? Existing accounts of retention explain persistence primarily through satisfaction, switching costs, or investments already made. We argue that consumer-AI relationships require a prospective theory of commitment: consumers may invest in the anticipated future value of a specific human-AI dyad. We introduce Anticipatory Relationship Investment (ARI), defined as deliberate cognitive and behavioral effort to create future relationship-specific value with an adaptive AI agent. ARI includes reusable prompts, instruction sets, structured context, feedback routines, and memory-building intended to improve future interactions. The Anticipatory Investment Model explains how credible capability trajectories and trajectory-based bonding motivate ARI, which converts present effort into relationship-specific capital, can increase psychological ownership, buffers dissatisfaction, and makes benchmark-superior alternatives appear less attractive when they lack dyad-specific context. The model specifies three boundary conditions: trajectory credibility, asset portability, and task identity relevance. It distinguishes ARI from sunk cost, escalation of commitment, learning costs, switching costs, psychological ownership, personalization lock-in, technology optimism, and brand attachment through divergent predictions about future-return salience, emotional tone, and response to trajectory disconfirmation.
