The framework contributes to relationship marketing, switching-cost theory, and service-dominant logic by showing how 2 adaptive AI can convert consumer labor into prospective relationship capital, creating genuine value but also welfare risks when firms restrict transparency, portability, or exit.
why: Consumer psychology with AI; not financial

title: AI-moderated Interviews for Market Research and Digital Twins Calibration
abstract: AI-moderated interviews are emerging as a scalable market-research method for generating consumer insights and building consumer "digital twins." Yet it remains unclear whether they match human-moderated interviews or improve on simpler, static data collection methods. In a pre-registered, between-subjects study (𝑁 = 317) with three industry partners, we compare AI-moderated (𝑁 = 154), human-moderated (𝑁 = 24), and static interviews (𝑁 = 154). AI moderation matches human moderation in depth, covers more themes, and, holding budget constant, recovers significantly more customer needs than human moderation or static interviews. However, participants sound more emotionally engaged when speaking to a live human. We then create digital twins using interview data and evaluate each twin against the participant's own held-out responses to six real-world marketing stimuli. We find that digital twins created from AI-moderated interviews predict consumer responses better than demographics-only personas. However, the additional richness from AI moderation does not translate into better quantitative predictions compared to static interviews. By analyzing open-ended thoughts generated from humans versus their twins, we find that prediction errors are connected both to differences in (self-reported) thinking styles between twins and humans, and to gaps between training and validation data (i.e., asking questions that are too far out of distribution).

title: From Dashboards to Autonomous Decisions: Artificial Intelligence Agents in Real-Time Financial Planning and Management Accounting
abstract: The emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the practice of management accounting in the support of economic decision-making processes in organisations. This study employs a conceptual research methodology to provide deeper insight into the role of agentic AI in the evolving landscape of management accounting. Guided by three complementary theories – structuration, sociomateriality, and institutional logics – we synthesise the literature to develop a multilayered conceptual framework explaining how autonomous AI agents alter financial planning routines. To help achieve the research objectives, the study draws on articles from five academic databases, government documents on AI ethics and standards, regulatory reports, and position papers from professional accounting bodies.

title: Compliance Is Not the Destination A Market-Entry Framework for AI Companies Built Outside Europe
abstract: Europe is one of the markets AI companies most want to enter, and one of the hardest to enter cleanly. Under the EU AI Act, a company does not need to be incorporated in the EU to fall within its scope: it is enough that a system is placed on the Union market, or that its output is used within the Union. For AI companies or AI solutions built in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, China, Singapore, Malaysia and elsewhere, this turns Europe from "another geography on the sales plan" into a distinct readiness problem. Most founders are asking the wrong question: "How do we comply with the AI Act?" , and find no shortage of answers: risk classifications, GPAI guidance, technical documentation rules, conformity assessment procedures. The European Commission continues to publish detailed guidance on all of it, which only reinforces how much founders now treat compliance as a moving target. The information is not the problem. The first problem is that none of it tells a founder what they actually need to know; the second problem is that they have the right answer to the wrong question. The right question is: "Given what we have built today, what has to change before we can credibly take this product into Europe?" This paper argues that EU AI compliance is not the destination, the EU AI market readiness is. It introduces the Lumo Compass Framework, a six-stage model that reframes market entry as an integrated product, regulatory and operational question, and closes with a short diagnostic any founder can run against their own product today.

title: Artificial intelligence and financial markets
abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming financial markets by enabling investors and intermediaries to extract more information from increasingly abundant data through advances in algorithms and computing power. We discuss how AI changes information production and decision-making, labor demand, and financial intermediation, with a particular emphasis on securities markets. We then survey the implications of this transformation for market efficiency, competition, informational frictions, and financial stability.

The strongest expectations associated with AI concern improved speed, ease of service use, consistency across channels and better identification of customer needs. By contrast, respondents are less convinced that AI can enhance empathy, emotional understanding, or the human dimensions of service delivery. Notably, most respondents indicate that AI-based virtual assistants are acceptable only when access to a human representative remains available. The study concludes that a meaningful gap exists between Generation Z's expectations and the customer experience currently offered in Georgia's financial sector. Although this generation is open to technological innovation, its acceptance of AI is conditional upon trust, transparency, security, and the continued availability of human touchpoints. Accordingly, AI should be viewed not as a substitute for human interaction, but as a complementary tool that can enhance efficiency, personalization, and responsiveness. title: Economy as a System of Actions: From Natural Economy to Market Self-Centralization
abstract: Standard general equilibrium theory treats coordination as something given a priori. Consequently, it lacks explanatory potential regarding the root causes of cyclical crises, accelerating inequality, and the institutional transformation of the market economy. This paper addresses a fundamental question: what is the specific mechanism through which a decentralized order culminates in the overcoming of decentralization itself? Rejecting the atomistic focus on an isolated subject, this study adopts the economic action as its primary unit of analysis, conceptualizing the economy as an integrated system of such actions. This framework allows for the synthesis of natural and market economies within a unified theoretical and methodological matrix. In a natural economy, the subject acts as a unitary locus of decision-making, coordinating production ex ante based on the direct knowledge of their own needs. Even in this embryonic form, one can discern the structural regularities that dictate the subsequent functioning of the market system. Market regulation emerges as the negation of centralized coordination: economic proportions are established in a decentralized fashion and ex post, given that actors produce goods for external agents whose needs resist a priori estimation. The alignment between production and consumption is achieved only post factum-mediated through price signals and profit mechanisms. The resulting imbalance between supply and demand is structural rather than merely quantitative, possessing an intrinsic asymmetry: while the need for commodities has a saturation threshold, the demand for liquidity (money) is inherently limitless. This transforms a chronic deficit of aggregate demand into an endogenous tendency of the system. This deficit is generated by inequality, masked by credit expansion, and drives the financialization of the economy, rendering the "Minsky moment" inevitable. Simultaneously, the immanent evolution of the market system-characterized by rising monopolization, the expansion of the financial sector, digitalization, the implementation of artificial intelligence, and the displacement of wage labor-drives a re-centralization of the economy contrary to its own foundational principles. This process constitutes a "negation of the negation," reinstating conscious ex ante coordination on a qualitatively higher plane. Whether the vector of this transformation unfolds through spontaneous crises or via conscious regulation remains an open question. The classical thesis regarding the informational impossibility of ex ante coordination was valid only for a bygone technological paradigm, where decentralization served as the sole viable form of alignment. However, as this paper demonstrates, contemporary technological conditions systematically erode these limitations. This paper serves as a synopsis of a comprehensive monographic study.

title: AI Token Budgets for Workers: Labor, Tax and Financial Treatment in Mexico
abstract: Some technology companies in the United States have started to give their engineers budgets of AI tokens, and whether those budgets are part of compensation is already under debate. The practice has barely reached Mexico, but Mexican law already contains the rules that would govern it. This paper argues that the legal treatment of a token budget depends mainly on how freely the worker can use the tokens, and proposes a four-level scale. At the first level the tokens can only be used for work; they are a work tool and do not form part of salary. At the second the worker may use them for personal purposes, and they become an in-kind benefit that forms part of salary and taxable income. At the third, a balance that can be spent across several providers resembles a grocery voucher, although the favorable voucher regime probably does not reach it. At the fourth the tokens can be transferred and used as payment, and only then could they fit the definition of virtual asset in the Fintech Law, provided the budget is not denominated in currency. At no level are tokens money. The Constitution requires wages to be paid in legal tender, and the Fintech Law distinguishes virtual assets from it. Tokens can be added to a salary, but cannot replace it. title: Litigation Finance and Its Discontents: Three Paradigms for an Emerging Market
abstract: Litigation finance has moved from a curiosity at the margins of American law into a billion-dollar market that creates serious dilemmas for claimants, law firms, and courts alike. This Article argues that “litigation finance” encompasses three distinct paradigms that raise different regulatory concerns: consumer financing for injured claimants, nonlawyer financing of law firms, and the financing of claim aggregation in mass-tort multidistrict litigation. Each of these paradigms demands a different regulatory response to varying degrees. But it is the third paradigm that presents the most urgent problem for our litigation landscape. The cost-reducing function of the MDL in combination with advertising-driven claim aggregation and presence of external capital has produced with this Article calls the “shadow portfolio”: large inventories of claims that have been identified and nominally retained but never filed, developed, or meaningfully scrutinized. Out of the court’s reach, these claims allow actors to gain influence over mass litigation without ever trying a case––a dynamic only accelerated by artificial intelligence. Reigning in the shadow portfolio will require reaching beyond the familiar regulatory toolkit––a difficult but necessary task to preserve the functionality of MDLs.

title: Who Benefits From Medical Innovation? Global Representation, Affordability, Safety and Regulatory Equity in Alzheimer's Disease and Cancer Research
abstract: Modern clinical research has produced striking advances in both Alzheimer's disease and cancer: the first disease-modifying Alzheimer's therapies, and an accelerating shift toward biomarker-gated precision oncology. Whether these advances reflect the global populations who carry the burden of these diseases, however, has rarely been measured directly rather than assumed. This monograph investigates that question using an original, purpose-built dataset: 400 interventional trials (200 per disease) randomly sampled from ClinicalTrials.gov, coded against a six-category exclusion-criteria taxonomy and scored using TREI-AC, an adaptation of the Trial Representation Equity Index built specifically for this comparison. Across the sample, 99.5% of Alzheimer's disease trials and 97.8% of cancer trials had no site in a country classified as low- or lower-middle-income by the World Bank; a two-tier comparison against disease-burden data shows trial-site presence in these countries running roughly 44 to 54 percentage points below their share of global disease burden for both conditions. Comorbidity and prior-treatment exclusion criteria were significantly more common in cancer trials than in Alzheimer's disease trials. In contrast, biomarker or imaging diagnostic requirements present in 15 to 16% of trials in both diseases structurally gate a meaningful share of research access behind infrastructure much of the world lacks. A dedicated case study of India-sited trials further distinguishes between an extractive pattern, in which a country functions only as a recruitment site within externally designed trials, and a domestic-research pattern largely disconnected from that same pipeline. Building on these findings, the monograph traces the same structural gap through diagnosis, treatment, affordability, pharmacovigilance, regulatory science, and the emerging role of artificial intelligence across the clinical research lifecycle, before proposing a ten-pillar Equity-by-Design framework and a disease-specific research agenda aimed at closing the gap this evidence documents. The central argument is that a therapy's value cannot be judged solely by whether it succeeds in the trial that produced it, if that trial was never positioned to reflect how it would perform for most of the people who will eventually need it.

title: Trading Metal for Lives: What Real-World Warfare Teaches About the Future of Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs)
abstract: The war in Ukraine has become the largest real-world testing ground for unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), stripping away exhibition-hall narratives and exposing what these systems actually do under fire. This paper distills five practical lessons from that experience and assesses their implications for defense markets and industrial strategy. First, the decisive contribution of UGVs has been logistical rather than kinetic: in the most contested sectors, ground robots now perform the majority of last-mile resupply and casualty evacuation, reducing infantry exposure. Second, full autonomy has largely given way to teleoperation, with artificial intelligence confined to a narrow assistive role and the human kept in the loop, particularly for weapons release. Third, the contested electromagnetic and aerial environment—saturated by reconnaissance and first-person-view (FPV) drones—has made survivability, not payload, the central design problem. Fourth, decentralized, rapid production created a severe standardization crisis, elevating component commonality, open architectures and forward repair to strategic priorities. Fifth, simple, rugged and attritable platforms have consistently outperformed expensive, complex ones. Taken together, these lessons reframe the UGV question away from the ultra-complex autonomous vehicle and toward inexpensive, robust, network-integrated ground tools designed to trade metal for lives. The paper concludes with implications for procurement, sustainment and the defense industrial base, with particular relevance to emerging markets seeking a realistic entry path into unmanned ground systems.

title: The Neurocomputational Cost of Cognitive Convenience : How Generative AI Reshapes the Biological Valuation of Effort
abstract: The brain is a metabolic optimizer that continuously evaluates whether the effort required to obtain a reward justifies the energy cost involved. This evaluation is regulated by dopamine within corticostriatal circuits and has been studied extensively through effort-based decision making paradigms, including the Effort Expenditure for Rewards Task (EEfRT) and the Apple Gathering Task (AGT). Generative artificial intelligence tools now offer a fundamentally different calculus: immediate, zero-effort answers to complex cognitive tasks. This narrative review proposes that habitual reliance on these tools may gradually recalibrate the brain's valuation of cognitive effort, producing consequences that resemble subclinical amotivation. We formalize this proposal through a hyperbolic discounting model of AI-mediated task delegation, in which the subjective value of AI-assisted output consistently exceeds that of effortful internal generation owing to near-zero external effort cost. Drawing on neurocomputational models of effort allocation, computational psychiatry findings from major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia, and emerging empirical research on human-AI interaction, we outline a mechanistic account of how cognitive convenience may erode effortful engagement over time. We apply the Opponent Actor Learning (OpAL) model as a neurobiological framework for understanding dopaminergic recalibration under chronic low-effort conditions, setting this framework against evidence from electroencephalographic studies, randomized controlled trials on retention, critical thinking surveys, and cognitive offloading research. We distinguish effortful cognitive engagement from passive AI delegation, review the neuroscience of retrieval practice and productive failure, and propose a research agenda together with practical recommendations for preserving effortful cognition within AI-integrated environments.

title: The Unorganised Market: Web Development and IT Services in India, 2026
abstract: India's web development sector is among the largest in the world by the number of people working in it, and among the least documented. This paper sets out what can be established from primary and semi-primary sources, meaning industry association data, judicial and regulatory records, platform-published rate data and directory listings, and separates that from the promotional material which currently stands in for market research on the subject. The argument is that the Indian web services market grew as a residue of two larger structures rather than under its own logic. The first is the offshore labour-arbitrage system built between 1968 and 2008. The second is the collapse of entry-level hiring in India's formal technology labour market after 2022. The paper then identifies the mechanisms behind the sector's persistent price dispersion, which are unobservable quality, near-zero entry barriers, absent contract enforcement and lead resale, and places them in the institutional conditions of Indian small business. It sets out a scenario analysis of what artificial intelligence is likely to do, stated without a prior in either direction, and closes with a selection rule for buyers facing a market in which quality cannot be observed before purchase.

title: High-Throughput Prediction of Si-X Bond Dissociation Energies via DFT-Trained Machine Learning: From Random Forest to Deep Neural Networks
abstract: It is crucial to accurately and rapidly calculate the bond dissociation energy of Si-X bonds as they determine the thermodynamic stability and reactivity of organosilicon compounds, which are significant in different chemistry fields. Although density functional theory calculations provide good estimates of BDEs, but their time-consuming nature renders the use of these methods for high-throughput screenings of molecular libraries unfeasible. The current work introduces a method based on the synergistic use of DFT and ML for predicting BDEs of different Si-X bond types: Si-C, Si-N, Si-O, Si-F, Si-H, Si-S, Si-Cl, Si-Br, Si-I, and Si-Si. A dataset of 1,200 organosilicon molecules was curated from PubChem database, and the BDEs were calculated with the UCAM-B3LYP/LANL2DZ level of theory, resulting in values ranging between 47.48 and 140.78 kcal mol⁻¹. Seven ML models were trained and thoroughly evaluated on an independent external test set of 200 compounds, including Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, Support Vector Regression (SVR), Shallow Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), and Custom Message-Passing Graph Neural Network (GNN) on molecular graph representation and Deep Regularized Neural Network (Deep NN). Deep NN provided the highest external test accuracy. UMAP visualization confirms that the set of descriptors contains information about both bond type identity and BDE value in the projected chemical space. Feature importance analysis found the sum of Si-X covalent radii and the index of bond polarity as the two most predictive descriptors. This approach reduces the time of BDE calculation from DFT computations by several orders of magnitude down to seconds and enables efficient high-throughput screening (HTS) of novel organosilicon compounds.

title: PDB-IHM: Methods for Programmatic Deposition of Integrative Structures to the Protein Data Bank
abstract: Integrative structure determination combines varied experimental information with computational modeling. We describe a programmatic workflow connecting the output of these calculations directly to deposition into the Protein Data Bank (PDB), a Worldwide Protein Data Bank Core Archive that now accommodates integrative or hybrid methods structures (PDB-IHM). The python-ihm package generates deposition-ready mmCIF files describing structure models, experimental restraints, modeling protocols, and their provenance. Subsequently, programmatic interfaces support pre-deposition validation, structure deposition, and processing status tracking. We illustrate the workflow using biostructure models derived from three-dimensional electron microscopy (3DEM) and crosslinking mass spectrometry (crosslinking-MS) information. We also demonstrate the workflow scalability through submission of a collection of crosslinking-MS structure models. Making structure validation and deposition machine-accessible in turn allows incorporation into high-throughput and AI-agent-driven structure-determination workflows. The workflow provides a reproducible and scalable pathway from integrative modeling to archival deposition.
